power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 7 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 21 R code files.
#### Run order

#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited. **14 data paths were built at runtime** with `sprintf()`/`paste()`/`file.path()` instead of written as a literal path — this is fragile authoring practice (it silently breaks if the code is run from a different working directory than the author's own). We resolved all of these on a best-effort basis.
#### Execution
**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 21 scripts: 17 ran without error, 2 errored, 2 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. **1 script stopped on a file another script writes**, so it was run once more after the other scripts: `simulation_infinite.R` (grid_manifest.txt). Which script must run first can be stated in a README, or shown by numbering the file names (01_, 02_).

text.text: Longitudinal assessments link test forms through common items.
Under item parameter drift, linked ability means and standard deviations depend on the item selection, adding a linking error (LE) to the standard error (SE).

Treating mean-geometric mean linking and pairwise Haberman linking across three time points in the two-parameter logistic model as M-estimators, this article derives closed-form LEs and sandwich estimators of LE, SE, and total error (TE).
Sandwich and item jackknife LE estimators are bias-corrected for person sampling, including dependent samples.

In a simulation study, SE-based intervals undercovered increasingly with sample size, bias-corrected jackknife TE intervals reached acceptable coverage almost everywhere, and sandwich-based intervals undercovered with few items.
Longitudinal mathematics data illustrate the estimators, with the LE exceeding the SE.

Educational large-scale assessments (LSAs) estimate trends and growth in student achievement with cognitive tests administered at several time points, in longitudinal designs as well as in repeated cross-sectional programs (e.g., Fischer et al., 2019; OECD, 2014).
text.formatted: Educational large-scale assessments (LSAs) estimate trends and growth in student achievement with cognitive tests administered at several time points, in longitudinal designs as well as in repeated cross-sectional programs (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Fischer et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">OECD, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Because the test forms differ across time points, a trend can be interpreted only after the results of all time points have been placed on a common scale through linking.

In the common-item nonequivalent groups design, each link connects two consecutive time points through the common items administered at both time points (Kolen & Brennan, 2014), and chain linking combines consecutive links to place a later time point on the common scale.
text.formatted: In the common-item nonequivalent groups design, each link connects two consecutive time points through the common items administered at both time points <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Kolen & Brennan, 2014)</ref>, and chain linking combines consecutive links to place a later time point on the common scale.

text.text: The design requires common items but not common persons, so the samples of the time points may be dependent, independent, or drawn from different populations.
Throughout, the two-parameter logistic (2PL) model for dichotomous items (Birnbaum, 1968) is assumed.
text.formatted: Throughout, the two-parameter logistic (2PL) model for dichotomous items <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Birnbaum, 1968</ref>) is assumed.

text.text: With the latent trait θ, referred to as the ability, and the response 𝑋 𝑖 to an item 𝑖, the probability of a correct response, 𝑋 𝑖 = 1, follows the item response function (IRF) with the item discrimination 𝑎 𝑖 , the item difficulty 𝑏 𝑖 , and the logistic function Ψ(𝑦) = exp (𝑦)/(1 + exp (𝑦)).
The trend is described by the linked means and standard deviations (SDs), the means and SDs of the ability distributions at the later time points on the common scale.
This article addresses the uncertainty that the selection of the common items and the sampling of persons contribute to the linked means and SDs.
Measurement invariance refers to equal item parameters of the common items across time points (Meredith, 1993; Millsap, 2011).
text.formatted: Measurement invariance refers to equal item parameters of the common items across time points <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Meredith, 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Millsap, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: If these item parameters differ, persons with equal θ have different probabilities of a correct response at different time points.

This longitudinal form of differential item functioning (DIF; Holland & Wainer, 1993; Mellenbergh, 1982) is called item parameter drift (IPD; Bock et al., 1988; Goldstein, 1983) and has repeatedly been found in the common items of operational assessments (e.g., Michaelides, 2010).
text.formatted: This longitudinal form of differential item functioning <ref type="bibr">(DIF;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Holland & Wainer, 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Mellenbergh, 1982)</ref> is called item parameter drift (IPD; <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Bock et al., 1988;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Goldstein, 1983)</ref> and has repeatedly been found in the common items of operational assessments (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Michaelides, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Uniform IPD changes only the item difficulties and shifts the IRF along the θ scale, whereas nonuniform IPD also changes the item discriminations, so that the shift varies with θ (Mellenbergh, 1982; Wells et al., 2002).
text.formatted: Uniform IPD changes only the item difficulties and shifts the IRF along the θ scale, whereas nonuniform IPD also changes the item discriminations, so that the shift varies with θ <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Mellenbergh, 1982;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">Wells et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: How IPD is treated depends on whether the item parameter changes are regarded as constructirrelevant or construct-relevant (Camilli, 1993; El Masri & Andrich, 2020).
text.formatted: How IPD is treated depends on whether the item parameter changes are regarded as constructirrelevant or construct-relevant <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Camilli, 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">El Masri & Andrich, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Construct-irrelevant changes bias the trend, so the affected items are typically revised, removed, or down-weighted (e.g., Engels et al., 2026b; Halpin, 2024; Penfield & Camilli, 2007), and only the items regarded as invariant define the common scale (Shealy & Stout, 1993).
text.formatted: Construct-irrelevant changes bias the trend, so the affected items are typically revised, removed, or down-weighted (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Engels et al., 2026b;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Halpin, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Penfield & Camilli, 2007)</ref>, and only the items regarded as invariant define the common scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b91">(Shealy & Stout, 1993)</ref>.

text.text: Construct-relevant changes arise, for example, when instruction places more emphasis on some content areas of the construct, so that their items become relatively easier at later time points (Bock et al., 1988; Zwitser et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Construct-relevant changes arise, for example, when instruction places more emphasis on some content areas of the construct, so that their items become relatively easier at later time points <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Bock et al., 1988;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b107">Zwitser et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Such item-specific parameter changes belong to the change that the trend describes, and removing the affected items would narrow the construct (El Masri & Andrich, 2020; Penfield & LINKING ERROR ACROSS MULTIPLE TIME POINTS Camilli, 2007; Robitzsch & Lüdtke, 2023; Zwitser et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Such item-specific parameter changes belong to the change that the trend describes, and removing the affected items would narrow the construct <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(El Masri & Andrich, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Penfield &</ref> LINKING ERROR ACROSS MULTIPLE TIME <ref type="bibr">POINTS Camilli, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">Robitzsch & Lüdtke, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b107">Zwitser et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Under the construct-relevant interpretation, IPD adds a source of uncertainty that the reported error should reflect (Robitzsch & Lüdtke, 2023) rather than disqualifying a trend, as is implied when invariance is treated as a prerequisite of longitudinal linking (e.g., Fischer et al., 2019; Wetzel & Carstensen, 2013).
text.formatted: Under the construct-relevant interpretation, IPD adds a source of uncertainty that the reported error should reflect <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">(Robitzsch & Lüdtke, 2023)</ref> rather than disqualifying a trend, as is implied when invariance is treated as a prerequisite of longitudinal linking (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Fischer et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b100">Wetzel & Carstensen, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: The present article adopts the construct-relevant interpretation and models the item-specific parameter changes, referred to as the IPD effects, as random draws from one distribution, whose variances, the IPD variances, quantify the magnitude of IPD (e.g., De Boeck, 2008; Longford et al., 1993; Robitzsch & Lüdtke, 2019; Van den Noortgate & De Boeck, 2005).
text.formatted: The present article adopts the construct-relevant interpretation and models the item-specific parameter changes, referred to as the IPD effects, as random draws from one distribution, whose variances, the IPD variances, quantify the magnitude of <ref type="bibr">IPD (e.g., De Boeck, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Longford et al., 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Robitzsch & Lüdtke, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Van den Noortgate & De Boeck, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Under IPD, the linked means and SDs depend on the selected common items, so the item selection adds variability beyond person sampling.

The linking error (LE; Michaelides & Haertel, 2014; Monseur & Berezner, 2007) quantifies this item-selection variability as the SD of a linked mean or a linked SD across replications of the random IPD effects of the common items.
text.formatted: The linking error (LE; <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Michaelides & Haertel, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Monseur & Berezner, 2007)</ref> quantifies this item-selection variability as the SD of a linked mean or a linked SD across replications of the random IPD effects of the common items.

text.text: This variability is often pictured as redrawing the items from a hypothetical pool (Michaelides & Haertel, 2014), as in generalizability theory and domain sampling (Brennan, 2001; Cronbach et al., 1972; McDonald, 2003), but the pool serves as a statistical tool, and no literal random selection of items is required (Robitzsch, 2023).
text.formatted: This variability is often pictured as redrawing the items from a hypothetical pool <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Michaelides & Haertel, 2014)</ref>, as in generalizability theory and domain sampling <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Brennan, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Cronbach et al., 1972;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">McDonald, 2003)</ref>, but the pool serves as a statistical tool, and no literal random selection of items is required <ref type="bibr">(Robitzsch, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Under an invariance assumption, this itemselection variability persists but is missing from the reported error (Robitzsch & Lüdtke, 2024).
text.formatted: Under an invariance assumption, this itemselection variability persists but is missing from the reported error <ref type="bibr">(Robitzsch & Lüdtke, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Person-sampling error is quantified by the standard error (SE), and the LE and the SE are combined in the total error (TE; e.g., Haberman et al., 2009; Xu & von Davier, 2010).
text.formatted: Person-sampling error is quantified by the standard error (SE), and the LE and the SE are combined in the total error (TE; e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Haberman et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b104">Xu & von Davier, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Because the LE does not decrease with the person sample size, it can reach or exceed the SE in LSAs with large person samples (Michaelides & Haertel, 2014; Monseur & Berezner, 2007; OECD, 2014), and ignoring it understates the error of a trend and inflates the Type I error rate of tests of trend differences (Monseur & Berezner, 2007; Wu, 2010).
text.formatted: Because the LE does not decrease with the person sample size, it can reach or exceed the SE in LSAs with large person samples <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Michaelides & Haertel, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Monseur & Berezner, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr">OECD, 2014)</ref>, and ignoring it understates the error of a trend and inflates the Type I error rate of tests of trend differences <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Monseur & Berezner, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b103">Wu, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: The LE studied here differs from the linking error of common-population designs, the person-sampling error of a link estimated from randomly equivalent samples rather than common items (Jewsbury, 2025a (Jewsbury, , 2025b; see also González & Wiberg, 2017).
text.formatted: The LE studied here differs from the linking error of common-population designs, the person-sampling error of a link estimated from randomly equivalent samples rather than common items <ref type="bibr">(Jewsbury, 2025a</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Jewsbury, , 2025b</ref>; see also <ref type="bibr">González & Wiberg, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: One line of work estimates the LE of a single link between two time points by resampling the common items, with the item jackknife or the bootstrap recomputing the linking from the item parameters of the reduced or resampled item sets (Haberman et al., 2009; Michaelides & Haertel, 2014; Monseur & Berezner, 2007).
text.formatted: One line of work estimates the LE of a single link between two time points by resampling the common items, with the item jackknife or the bootstrap recomputing the linking from the item parameters of the reduced or resampled item sets <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Haberman et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Michaelides & Haertel, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Monseur & Berezner, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: The double jackknife and the double bootstrap resample persons and items together and remove the person-sampling share from the item-level variability by subtraction (Battauz, 2017; Haberman et al., 2009; Xu & von Davier, 2010), and hierarchical models with random item effects treat both sources of variability in one model (De Boeck, 2008; Fox & Verhagen, 2010).
text.formatted: The double jackknife and the double bootstrap resample persons and items together and remove the person-sampling share from the item-level variability by subtraction <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Battauz, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Haberman et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b104">Xu & von Davier, 2010)</ref>, and hierarchical models with random item effects treat both sources of variability in one model <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(De Boeck, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Fox & Verhagen, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: For the simultaneous linking of multiple forms, Battauz (2017) derived SEs based on the delta method for the estimated links under invariant item parameters and estimated the item-selection variability with such a double bootstrap.
text.formatted: For the simultaneous linking of multiple forms, <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Battauz (2017)</ref> derived SEs based on the delta method for the estimated links under invariant item parameters and estimated the item-selection variability with such a double bootstrap.

text.text: Resampling quantifies the LE in a given assessment but does not show how the IPD variances and the numbers of common items determine it, which closed-form expressions make explicit.

In the one-parameter logistic (1PL) model under mean-mean linking, where the linked means are linear in the IPD effects, LINKING ERROR ACROSS MULTIPLE TIME POINTS such closed forms were obtained from variance components of the item difficulty differences between two time points (Monseur & Berezner, 2007) and for trend estimates (Robitzsch & Lüdtke, 2019 , 2023).
text.formatted: In the one-parameter logistic (1PL) model under mean-mean linking, where the linked means are linear in the IPD effects, LINKING ERROR ACROSS MULTIPLE TIME POINTS such closed forms were obtained from variance components of the item difficulty differences between two time points <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Monseur & Berezner, 2007)</ref> and for trend estimates <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">(Robitzsch & Lüdtke, 2019</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In the 2PL model, the linked means and SDs are nonlinear in the IPD effects.

Using M-estimation theory (Boos & Stefanski, 2013; Huber, 1981; Stefanski & Boos, 2002) and the delta method, subsequent work derived closed forms for mean-geometric mean (MGM) chain linking across three time points (Robitzsch, 2023) and LEs for pairwise Haberman linking (PHL) across multiple groups (Robitzsch, 2025a).
text.formatted: Using M-estimation theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Boos & Stefanski, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Huber, 1981;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">Stefanski & Boos, 2002)</ref> and the delta method, subsequent work derived closed forms for mean-geometric mean (MGM) chain linking across three time points <ref type="bibr">(Robitzsch, 2023)</ref> and LEs for pairwise Haberman linking (PHL) across multiple groups <ref type="bibr">(Robitzsch, 2025a)</ref>.

text.text: For two groups, which correspond to two time points, the SE, the TE, and a bias-corrected LE were added (Robitzsch, 2024b).
text.formatted: For two groups, which correspond to two time points, the SE, the TE, and a bias-corrected LE were added <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">(Robitzsch, 2024b)</ref>.

text.text: However, no decomposition into LE, SE, and TE that treats item selection and person sampling simultaneously exists for MGM and PHL with more than two time points, the bias-corrected LE has not been extended to chain linking, and sandwich-based and jackknife LEs have not been compared for PHL.

Such a decomposition must account for the items administered at all time points, which enter several links and thereby induce covariances among the linked means and SDs of different time points, and for the dependence of longitudinal person samples.

The present article derives this decomposition for MGM and PHL under the 2PL model by casting both linking methods in one M-estimation framework (Boos & Stefanski, 2013; Huber, 1981; Stefanski & Boos, 2002), which also shows how their LEs differ.
text.formatted: The present article derives this decomposition for MGM and PHL under the 2PL model by casting both linking methods in one M-estimation framework <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Boos & Stefanski, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Huber, 1981;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">Stefanski & Boos, 2002)</ref>, which also shows how their LEs differ.

text.text: The M-estimation framework holds for any number of time points, and the closed forms are given for three time points, the smallest design in which links are chained and common items enter several links.

Both linking methods operate directly on the item parameters from the separate calibration of each time point, and their trend estimates remained less biased under random DIF and IPD than those of concurrent calibration and of the Haebara (Haebara, 1980) and Stocking-Lord (Stocking & Lord, 1983) methods (Engels et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Both linking methods operate directly on the item parameters from the separate calibration of each time point, and their trend estimates remained less biased under random DIF and IPD than those of concurrent calibration and of the Haebara <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Haebara, 1980)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">Stocking-Lord (Stocking & Lord, 1983</ref>) methods <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Engels et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Concurrent calibration assumes measurement invariance, and the nonlinear criteria of the Haebara and Stocking-Lord methods imply a bias that vanishes neither with more persons nor with more items (Engels et al., 2025; Robitzsch, 2024a).
text.formatted: Concurrent calibration assumes measurement invariance, and the nonlinear criteria of the Haebara and Stocking-Lord methods imply a bias that vanishes neither with more persons nor with more items <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Engels et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Robitzsch, 2024a)</ref>.

text.text: MGM links consecutive time points through means of these item parameters and combines these links by chain linking (Kolen & Brennan, 2014; Mislevy & Bock, 1990), whereas PHL estimates the linked means and SDs of all later time points simultaneously from all pairs of time points (Haberman, 2009; Robitzsch, 2025a).
text.formatted: MGM links consecutive time points through means of these item parameters and combines these links by chain linking <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Kolen & Brennan, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Mislevy & Bock, 1990)</ref>, whereas PHL estimates the linked means and SDs of all later time points simultaneously from all pairs of time points <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Haberman, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Robitzsch, 2025a)</ref>.

text.text: The LE is estimated with sandwich estimators and the item jackknife, and bias corrections remove the person-sampling share from these estimates.
Two estimators of the sampling covariance of the item parameters, a stacked calibration and a person bootstrap, extend the SE and the bias corrections to dependent person samples.

A simulation study with independent person samples evaluates the estimators, and longitudinal mathematics data from three grades of one cohort illustrate them, including the dependent-sample extension.
The Discussion closes with recommendations for practice.
This section casts longitudinal linking with 𝑇 time points as an M-estimation problem, derives the LE, the SE, and the TE of the linked means and SDs, and extends them to dependent person samples.

In M-estimation, an estimator solves estimating equations that sum item-level contributions (Stefanski & Boos, 2002), so the LE and the SE follow from linear expansions of these equations, with the IPD effects and the person-sampling errors as the two sources of variability.
text.formatted: In M-estimation, an estimator solves estimating equations that sum item-level contributions <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">(Stefanski & Boos, 2002)</ref>, so the LE and the SE follow from linear expansions of these equations, with the IPD effects and the person-sampling errors as the two sources of variability.

text.text: Detailed derivations and additional simulation results are given in the Supplement, and equations, tables, and figures with the prefix S refer to it.
At time point 𝑡 = 1, . . . , 𝑇, the abilities follow the normal distribution N(µ 𝑡 , σ 2 𝑡 ) with the mean µ 𝑡 and the SD σ 𝑡 .
Under local independence, the marginal probability of a response pattern is the integral of the product of the IRFs (Eq. 1) over this distribution.

In separate calibration, the 2PL model ( Eq. 1)is fitted to the responses of each time point on its own, and the means and SDs of the later time points, the linked parameters, are then determined through linking on the scale of the first time point (T1), the T1 scale, which serves as the reference scale.

The item jackknife (JK; e.g., Haberman et al., 2009; Monseur & Berezner, 2007; cf. text.text: For dependent samples, V ˆ︁ γ is estimated by a stacked calibration or by a person bootstrap.
The stacked calibration treats the 𝑇 separate calibrations as one M-estimation problem in which the persons are the independent units.
The estimating functions are the calibration scores, the derivatives of each person's marginal log-likelihood contribution with respect to the item parameters (Eqs.
S3 to S5).
The bread matrix of the stacked calibration is block diagonal, with one block per separate calibration (Eq.
S4), so the dependence between time points enters only through the off-diagonal blocks of its meat matrix (Eq.
S5), which sum the products of the calibration scores of the shared persons at two time points.
The person bootstrap draws samples of size 𝑁 ∪ with replacement from the union sample and keeps each person's complete responses and participation pattern z 𝑛 = (𝑧 𝑛1 , . . . , 𝑧 𝑛𝑇 ) ⊤ .

Each replicate is recalibrated at every time point, and V ˆ︁ γ is estimated by the empirical covariance matrix of the calibrated item parameters across the 𝑅 boot replicates (Efron & Tibshirani, 1994).
text.formatted: Each replicate is recalibrated at every time point, and V ˆ︁ γ is estimated by the empirical covariance matrix of the calibrated item parameters across the 𝑅 boot replicates <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Efron & Tibshirani, 1994)</ref>.

text.text: The stacked calibration and the person bootstrap assume that participation does not depend on the abilities (Rubin, 1976).

text.text: Selective nonresponse biases the calibrated item parameters themselves and is not handled in this treatment.
Because the abilities of the shared persons are typically positively correlated over time, so are the sampling errors of the calibrated item parameters at different time points.

The estimating functions contrast the calibrated item parameters of the same item at two time points, such as log ˆ︁ 𝑎 𝑖2log ˆ︁ 𝑎 𝑖1 , so the correlated sampling errors partly cancel in these differences.
Treating dependent samples as independent therefore tends to overstate the SE (Jewsbury, 2025b; Kolen & Brennan, 2014; Liou & Cheng, 1995).

text.text: All covariances in 𝚽 were thus zero, so the item parameters followed the random walk (Eq. 3) from the first administration of each item onward, and the items of 𝐶 2:3 received their first IPD effects at T3.
The IPD effects were drawn from normal distributions or, with heavier tails at the same variances, from 𝑡 distributions with three degrees of freedom (𝑡 3 ), scaled by √︁ 1/3.
The condition without IPD and the two IPD levels under each of the two distributions gave five IPD conditions.
Crossed with the three numbers of items and the four sample sizes, they yielded 60 cells.

Every cell used 𝑅 = 4000 replications, with the IPD effects redrawn in each replication, which puts the Monte Carlo standard error of a coverage rate at the nominal level at 0.34 percentage points (Morris et al., 2019).

text.text: With finite person samples, independent person samples were drawn at each time point 𝑡 from N(µ 𝑡 , σ 2 𝑡 ), and the item responses were generated from the 2PL model.

Each time point was then calibrated separately by marginal maximum likelihood with the expectation-maximization algorithm (Bock & Aitkin, 1981), under the identifying restriction θ ∼ N(0, 1) and with the estimated item discriminations bounded below at 0.1, so that near-zero estimates do not produce extreme log item discriminations in the links.

text.text: MGM was applied as chain linking and PHL with the item weights ω 𝑖 = 𝐼/𝑚 𝑖 .
For all four linked parameters, µ 2 , σ 2 , µ 3 , and σ 3 , the ESW, the BOSW, and the JK were computed in every replication.
With finite person samples, the SE, the LE bc estimates, the TE, and TE bc were added.
The linked estimates were evaluated by their bias and root mean square error (RMSE) across the replications.

LE estimates were summarized by cell medians rather than means, because LE estimates, as SDs computed from few items, were right-skewed within a cell, and an LE bc estimate is set to zero whenever the bias correction yields a negative LE variance.

With infinite person samples, the recovery of the item-selection variability was assessed by the ratio of the median LE estimate in a cell to the true LE of the cell, with the ideal value one (Morris et al., 2019).

text.text: With finite person samples, the median LE estimate in a cell was compared with its median under infinite person samples in the same IPD condition and with the same number of common items.
This difference isolates the person-sampling share, and absolute differences above 0.01 are marked in the tables.

Coverage was evaluated for the 95% intervals of the linked parameters, formed by the linked estimate ±1.96 times its LE estimate (infinite person samples) or its estimated SE, TE, or TE bc (finite person samples).
Coverage rates between 92.5% and 97.5% were classified as acceptable, based on the rates rounded to one decimal place as they are reported.

A variance decomposition of the binary indicator of unacceptable coverage, which treats undercoverage and overcoverage alike, quantified the shares of the simulation factors and their interactions (Table S17), and Figure 2 shows all coverage rates of the TE-and TE bc -based intervals for ˆ︁ µ 3 and ˆ︁ σ 3 as a specification curve (Simonsohn et al., 2020).

text.text: With finite person samples, the SE-based intervals reached the nominal level without IPD but undercovered in every cell with IPD, because the SE omits the LE, whose share of the TE grows with the sample size.
Larger samples therefore aggravate this undercoverage.
Under strong normal IPD at 𝐼 = 15, the coverage under MGM fell from 67.8% at 𝑁 = 500 to 39.9% at 𝑁 = 2000, whereas the interval based on the TE bc of the JK covered in 95.0% and 95.1%.

The TE-based intervals overcovered wherever the true LE is small relative to the person-sampling share of the LE estimate, that is, in nearly all cells without IPD, with up to 99.2%, and in a few cells with weak IPD.
Without IPD, the overcoverage decreased with the number of items but not with the sample size, because the person-sampling share and the SE shrink at the same rate.
With the bias correction, this overcoverage disappeared.

The intervals based on the TE bc of the JK stayed within the acceptable range in all cells, whereas those based on the TE bc of the sandwich estimators undercovered at 𝐼 = 15, mainly under PHL and down to 90.8%, in line with the overcorrection of their bias corrections.
Under strong 𝑡 3 IPD, the results resembled those under strong normal IPD (Table S4).

The intervals based on the TE bc of the JK stayed within the acceptable range in all but one cell (92.4% for PHL under strong normal IPD at 𝐼 = 15 and 𝑁 = 1000), and those based on the TE bc of the sandwich estimators undercovered down to 89.5% (Table S7).

text.text: The example uses the mathematics assessment of students in the academic track (Gymnasium) at the beginning of Grade 7 in 2005 (T1), the end of Grade 8 in 2007 (T2), and the beginning of Grade 11 in 2009 (T3).
To protect participant confidentiality, the example uses a synthetic data set generated by data-augmented multiple imputation (Grund et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2022).
text.formatted: To protect participant confidentiality, the example uses a synthetic data set generated by data-augmented multiple imputation <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Grund et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Jiang et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The procedure imputes the responses by partial least squares regression and adds random noise with the noise parameter 0.3, so that the synthetic data retain the distributional structure of the original responses.
Because the three time points followed one student cohort, the person samples were dependent.
Of the 𝑁 ∪ = 6970 students of the union sample, 𝑁 𝑡 = 4521, 5263, and 5152 were assessed at T1, T2, and T3, and 2996 at all three time points.
The numbers of shared persons were 𝑁12 = 3863, 𝑁23 = 3948, and 𝑁13 = 3151.
Of the 139 mathematics items, 36 served as common items, with 12 in 𝐶 1:3 , 10 in 𝐶 1:2 , and 14 in 𝐶 2:3 , so that 𝐼12 = 22, 𝐼23 = 26, and 𝐼123 = 12 (Figure S1).

text.text: The items were distributed across booklets in a multiple-matrix sampling design (Frey et al., 2009; Rutkowski et al., 2014), and each common item was answered by 1071 to 5263 students at a time point.

The SE was computed with the stacked calibration (SE st ), with the person bootstrap (SE boot ), and under the assumption of independent person samples (SE ind ), and each of the three entered its own TE and TE bc.
All three separate calibrations and all 𝑅 boot = 2000 bootstrap recalibrations converged.

text.text: Under MGM, the mathematics achievement of the cohort increased by ˆ︁ µ2 = 0.74 from Grade 7 to Grade 8 and by ˆ︁ µ3 = 1.40 from Grade 7 to Grade 11 on the T1 scale, while the SD remained close to one (ˆ︁ σ2 = 1.03, ︁ σ3 = 0.95).

PHL gave slightly smaller growth estimates, ˆ︁ µ2 = 0.72 and ˆ︁ µ3 = 1.36, but the differences to MGM were small relative to the TE bc,st of the JK, which was 0.11 for ˆ︁ µ 2 and 0.18 for ˆ︁ µ 3 under MGM.
The LE estimates of all three estimators exceeded the SEs for all linked parameters.
For ︁ µ 3 under MGM, the JK LE was 0.182, compared with an SE st of 0.048 and an SE boot of 0.050.
At the given sample sizes, the uncertainty of the linked means was therefore dominated by the selection of the common items rather than by person sampling (Michaelides & Haertel, 2014).

text.text: For ˆ︁ σ 2 and ˆ︁ σ 3 , the LE estimates were smaller in absolute terms but still about twice the SEs.

The three LE estimates agreed closely, with the sandwich estimates slightly below the JK estimate, and the bias corrections reduced the LE estimates only modestly, because the large person samples imply a small person-sampling share of the variability across items.
For ˆ︁ µ 3 under MGM, LE bc,st ranged from 0.168 (BOSW) to 0.177 (JK) and TE bc,st from 0.174 to 0.183, which gave 95% intervals of about 1.40 ± 0.35.

Here, TE bc,st slightly exceeded the uncorrected LE estimate for all three estimators, so the SE added back more than the correction had removed, and the uncorrected TE st , 0.180 to 0.188, lay above both.
For the sandwich estimators, this is consistent with positive between-item sampling covariances, which the SE contains (Eq.
11) but the item-diagonal correction (Eq. 13) omits.
The LE estimates of PHL exceeded those of MGM for all four parameters and all three estimators, for example, 0.213 versus 0.182 for the JK LE of ˆ︁ µ 3 .
Under the random walk, this ordering is the expected one, and the differences of the linked item parameters between consecutive administrations indicate which IPD process the data support.

text.text: This article cast MGM and PHL as M-estimation problems for any number of time points and derived the LE, the SE, and the TE of the linked means and SDs, together with bias corrections for person sampling and an extension to dependent person samples.
The closed forms make the role of the cross-link covariances of the IPD effects explicit, and the simulation compared the two linking methods and the three LE estimators under the same conditions.
With infinite person samples, the JK reached acceptable coverage in all cells, whereas the sandwich estimators undercovered at the smallest number of common items, more strongly under PHL.

With finite person samples, the bias corrections removed the person-sampling share from the LE estimates, and the intervals based on the TE bc of the JK reached acceptable coverage in all cells but one.

The bias corrections of the sandwich estimators overcorrected at 𝐼 = 15, so their intervals undercovered there, consistent with the between-item sampling terms that the item-diagonal correction omits.
The SE-based intervals undercovered in every condition with IPD, and this undercoverage grew with the sample size (Monseur & Berezner, 2007; Wu, 2010).
text.formatted: The SE-based intervals undercovered in every condition with IPD, and this undercoverage grew with the sample size <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Monseur & Berezner, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b103">Wu, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: In the empirical example, the LE estimates exceeded the SEs for all linked parameters, and those of PHL exceeded those of MGM, most strongly for ˆ︁ µ 3 .
Under equal IPD variances and zero cross-link covariances, the closed forms predict an excess of only about 5% in this design (Eqs. 21, 22, 26, and 27).
text.formatted: Under equal IPD variances and zero cross-link covariances, the closed forms predict an excess of only about 5% in this design <ref type="bibr">(Eqs. 21,</ref> <ref type="bibr">22,</ref> <ref type="bibr">26,</ref> <ref type="bibr">and 27)</ref>.

text.text: The remainder cannot be separated from the variability of the LE estimates in a single data set, which the simulation showed to be larger under PHL.
Because the IPD process of an assessment is unknown, the choice between the linking methods implies an assumption about this process.
Under the random walk, MGM yields the smaller LE in this design.
PHL can yield the smaller LE when the cross-link covariances are sufficiently negative (Eq.

S9), and it gains relative to MGM with items that skip T2, which only the direct time-point pair T1 ↔ T3 uses, and when person sampling dominates, because this time-point pair is free of the sampling error of the T2 calibration.
The simulation used one connected design with common-item sets of equal size, normal ability distributions, equal sample sizes at all time points, and IPD effects with zero covariances.

Common-item sets of unequal size and unequal sample sizes across time points, as they arise from attrition in longitudinal studies, are next steps, because both the number of common items and the sample size affect the variability of chained equating coefficients (cf. Battauz, 2015).

text.text: IPD processes with nonzero cross-link covariances are a further step, for which the closed forms indicate where differences between the linking methods should appear.

Samples smaller than those studied here, such as 𝑁 = 250, raise the person-sampling share of the variation across items, so the bias corrections and the truncation at zero matter more and need their own evaluation.
The extension to dependent person samples was illustrated but not evaluated by simulation.
Varying the numbers 𝑁 𝑡𝑡 ′ of shared persons and the correlation of the abilities across time points would show how far the stacked calibration and the person bootstrap recover the SE and LE bc.
The SE treated the students as independent draws, although they are nested in schools.
Summing the calibration scores of the students within schools in the meat matrix of the stacked calibration (Eq.
S5), as in cluster-robust sandwich estimators (Liang & Zeger, 1986), or using replication weights (Wu, 2010) would typically enlarge the SE.

text.text: The uncorrected LE estimates would not change, because they use only the calibrated item parameters.
The M-estimation framework also assumes IPD effects that are independent across items.

If IPD is also a property of the testlet for items that share a stimulus (Monseur et al., 2008; Wainer et al., 2007), the testlet replaces the item as the independent unit, so the meat matrix sums over testlets and the JK deletes one testlet at a time (Monseur & Berezner, 2007).

text.text: Finally, the decomposition of the TE into the SE and the LE rests on the independence of item selection and person sampling, which is not guaranteed when test forms are assigned by prior achievement or in adaptive testing, where the administered items depend on the abilities of the assessed persons (Fink et al., 2025).

text.text: Beyond the item weights, the criteria of PHL could weight the time-point pairs, for example, with weights that decrease with the distance between the time points, which would down-weight the direct time-point pair T1 ↔ T3, whose items carry the sums of the IPD effects of both links.

Mean-mean linking fits the same M-estimation framework (Loyd & Hoover, 1980), but because the random walk (Eq. 3) acts on the log item discriminations, it holds their geometric rather than their arithmetic mean constant, which matches MGM.

text.text: Under the assumptions of the M-estimation framework, the results suggest reporting the trend with the LE bc of the JK, the SE, and TE bc .
These assumptions include IPD effects that are independent across items and participation that does not depend on the abilities.

The JK recomputes the complete linking for every deleted item and thereby captures the item-selection variability of the estimator without the asymptotic approximation of the sandwich estimators, which explains why its intervals reached acceptable coverage at small numbers of items and under heavy-tailed IPD.

Its costs are the 𝐼 recomputations per linking and a person-sampling bias correction that requires the full sampling covariance matrix of the calibrated item parameters LINKING ERROR ACROSS MULTIPLE TIME POINTS (Eq.
S1), which the stacked calibration or the person bootstrap provides for dependent person samples.

Because the sandwich-based intervals undercovered at 𝐼 = 15 and under PHL in part also at 𝐼 = 30, designs with at least 30 common items appear advisable when the sandwich estimators are used, in line with the general advice to raise the number of common items in LSAs (Mazzeo & von Davier, 2008; Weeks et al., 2014).

The closed forms remain useful at the design stage, because they show how the common-item counts 𝐼 12 , 𝐼 23 , and 𝐼 123 and the IPD variances determine the LE before data are collected.

Reporting both MGM and PHL, as in the empirical example, makes the sensitivity of the trend and its LE to the IPD process visible and treats the choice of the linking method as a further source of uncertainty, the model uncertainty (Longford, 2012).

If every common item is administered at all three time points, all three time-point pairs contribute to PHL, and the direct time-point pair T1 ↔ T3 compares the sums 𝑓 𝑖2 + 𝑓 𝑖3 and 𝑒 𝑖2 + 𝑒 𝑖3 of the IPD effects of both links.
All items share the item weight ω 𝑖 = 𝐼/3, so the weighting leaves the estimates unchanged.
Because every time-point pair is computed over the same complete item set, the pairwise condition of any two time points follows by adding the conditions of the links between them.
The chain solution therefore satisfies the first-order conditions of the PHL criteria in Equation ( 23), and PHL reproduces the MGM estimates for both links.
text.formatted: The chain solution therefore satisfies the first-order conditions of the PHL criteria in Equation ( <ref type="formula" target="#formula_25">23</ref>), and PHL reproduces the MGM estimates for both links.

text.text: In both designs, the two methods therefore define the same estimator, so they share the same LE and the same JK estimate.
The sandwich estimators coincide as well.

Under the reparameterization s3 = s 2 + s 2,3 and µ3 = µ 2 + σ 2 µ 2,3 , the PHL estimating function of each item is a linear transformation of its MGM estimating function, with a matrix that depends only on δ and is the same for all items.

Because the estimating functions sum to zero at the estimate, the bread matrix, the meat matrix, and the sampling meat matrices transform accordingly, and the PHL sandwich variances equal the delta-method transforms of the MGM sandwich variances.
The SE, LE bc , and the TE therefore agree as well.
For two time points and 𝐼 common items, the parameter vector is δ = (s 2 , µ 2 ) ⊤ .

With a single pair, every common item has the item weight ω 𝑖 = 𝐼/2, which cancels, and the first-order conditions of the PHL criteria are the MGM estimating equations, so PHL coincides with MGM (Engels et al., 2025).

text.text: The interaction of the IPD condition with the bias correction accounted for the largest share (22% and 25% for ˆ︁ µ 3 and ˆ︁ σ 3 ).

Further shares fell to the IPD condition (13% and 12%), the number of items (8% and 5%), and, for ˆ︁ σ 3 , the bias correction (15%), whereas the sample size, the LE estimator, and the linking method each accounted for at most 1%.

The largest three-way terms were the interactions of the IPD condition with the number of items and the bias correction (3.4% and 2.2% for ˆ︁ µ 3 and ˆ︁ σ 3 ), with the number of items and the sample size (2.0% and 1.1%), with the sample size and the bias correction (1.7% and 1.6%), and, for ˆ︁ σ 3 , with the sample size and the LE estimator (1.5%).
No other three-way term exceeded 1.5%, so the three-way structure mainly refines the dominant interaction of the IPD condition with the bias correction.

Dependent Person Samples The separate calibrations estimate the sampling covariance matrix V ˆ︁ γ of the calibrated item parameters without sampling covariances between time points, which is correct under independent person samples.

In many longitudinal designs, the same persons are assessed repeatedly, and the samples overlap only partially, because persons drop out, enter the study later, or are absent at individual time points.

With the participation indicator 𝑧 𝑛𝑡 = 1 if person 𝑛 is assessed at time point 𝑡 and 𝑧 𝑛𝑡 = 0 otherwise, the union sample collects the 𝑁 ∪ = ∑︁ 𝑛 max 𝑡 𝑧 𝑛𝑡 persons assessed at least once, and 𝑁 𝑡 = ∑︁ 𝑛 𝑧 𝑛𝑡 of them are assessed at time point 𝑡.
The 𝑁 𝑡𝑡 ′ = ∑︁ 𝑛 𝑧 𝑛𝑡 𝑧 𝑛𝑡 ′ persons assessed at both 𝑡 and 𝑡 ′ ≠ 𝑡, referred to as shared persons, make the cross-time-point blocks of V ˆ︁ γ nonzero.

Only the estimate of V ˆ︁ γ changes, so the SE, LE bc , and the TE (Eqs. 11 to 15) are computed with the same formulas, whereas the LE estimates without bias correction do not depend on V ˆ︁ γ at all.
